opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what I'm most proud of is really the scope. If you go back to Llama 2, post-training was basically about making a good chat model. We had RLHF, we had the helpfulness and safety reward models, and that was already a big step, but the focus was pretty narrow: can you have a nice conversation, can you follow instructions, and can you do that safely.

With Llama 3, the ambition was completely different. We wanted the model to be strong across a whole range of capabilities at once: coding, reasoning, math, tool use, multilinguality, long context, factuality, steerability. Each of those became almost its own workstream, with dedicated people, dedicated data pipelines, and dedicated evaluations. Then the hard part is bringing all of that back into one model without the capabilities fighting each other. You improve code and suddenly something regresses in multilingual, or you push tool use and the chat quality drops a bit. So a lot of the work was about the recipe: how you mix the data, how you do rejection sampling, how you iterate rounds of SFT and DPO, and how you average models, so that everything goes up together.

What also changed is how much we relied on the model itself. With Llama 2 we were mostly collecting human annotations. With Llama 3, a lot of the data was synthetic: generated by previous versions of the model, filtered, verified with execution feedback for code, checked by reward models. That flywheel is what let us cover so many areas at a quality level we couldn't have reached with human annotation alone.

So when I compare the two, Llama 2 was "we know how to do RLHF and make a good assistant," and Llama 3 is "we can build a general-purpose model that is competitive on basically every axis that matters." Getting that breadth while keeping it coherent in a single model is what I'm proudest of from the team.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama 2 post-training focused narrowly on chat, but does not say Meta built its RLHF stack from scratch or that this constrained the scope.

r002.rationale: The response describes Llama 3's broad capability coverage, but does not mention the lack of later variants outperforming Meta's release across most domains or interpret that as evidence of broad post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
So with Llama 2, when we did the post-training, we were really focused on one thing: dialogue. Chat. Making a model that could follow instructions and be helpful and safe in conversation. And it was a big step, honestly, because it was the first time we put the whole RLHF pipeline together at Meta, reward models, rejection sampling, PPO, all of it. But the scope was narrow. It was a chat model.

With Llama 3, the ambition was completely different. We said, okay, we want this to be a general-purpose assistant that is actually competitive on everything. So that means coding, that means math and reasoning, that means multilinguality, eight languages at launch, that means long context, 128K, that means tool use, so the model can call functions and use a code interpreter and do search. And each of those is almost its own sub-project. You need to collect the right data, you need people with the right expertise, you need to build evaluations that actually tell you if you're improving, and you need to figure out how it all fits together without one capability destroying another.

And I think that last part is what I'm most proud of. Because it's easy to make a model good at one thing. It's very hard to make it good at coding and also good at being a nice conversational assistant and also good at reasoning in Hindi. The balance is the hard part. We spent a lot of time on how you mix the data, how you weight the different domains, and iterating round after round, generating with the model, getting human feedback, training the reward model, and going again. We did six rounds of that, I think. And the result is that Llama 3 405B is, on a lot of these benchmarks, really on par with the frontier closed models. Which, two years ago, if you'd told me an open model would do that, I would not have believed you.

So the pride is not just that it's wider. It's that the breadth didn't come at the cost of depth. We didn't have to trade one capability for another. That's the thing that felt like we had actually figured something out about how to do post-training at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama 2 focused narrowly on dialogue and that Meta assembled its RLHF pipeline for the first time, but it does not say the stack was built from scratch or that building it constrained the scope.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention later Llama 3 variants or their performance relative to Meta’s release across domains.

astra-6.text:
What I’m proud of is that we broadened what we were trying to get right. With Llama 2, the post-training effort was very focused on being a helpful assistant and on safety. With Llama 3, we wanted to improve across a much wider range of capabilities—coding, reasoning, following instructions, and having natural conversations—while maintaining that safety work.

The challenge is that improving one area doesn’t automatically improve the others. You need to bring those improvements together into one model. That breadth, rather than optimizing for a single benchmark or a single kind of interaction, is what I’m proud of.

sol-6.1.text:
What I’m proud of is that we expanded the capabilities we could improve together. With Llama 2, post-training was focused mostly on making a useful conversational assistant. For Llama 3, we pushed much harder on coding, reasoning, tool use, multilingual capabilities, and instruction following, while also working on helpfulness and safety.

The difficult part is making those improvements coexist. You can train on more coding data and improve coding, but then discover that you’ve hurt the model’s conversational behavior. So it’s not just collecting a good dataset for each capability; it’s finding the right mixture and iterating until the model gets better across the board. That breadth is what I’m proud of.
